# Sex determination and sex-linked disorders

## 1. Introduction

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Sex determination and sex-linked disorders

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

In humans and most mammals, sex is fixed at fertilisation by the sex chromosomes: **XX** = female, **XY** = male. The Y chromosome carries **SRY**, the master switch that turns the embryonic gonads into testes; without it, development defaults to female. Because the X carries hundreds of genes the Y lacks, alleles on the X show **sex-linked inheritance**: a recessive allele that a heterozygous mother carries shows itself in sons, who have only one X.

**Concept flow — from chromosomes to haemophilia (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sex chromosomes vs autosomes | 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes in humans |
| 2 | XX / XY system | The ovum is always X; the sperm is X or Y — the father determines sex |
| 3 | SRY gene on Y | Triggers testis development; without it, ovaries form |
| 4 | X-linked recessive inheritance | Haemophilia A, colour blindness — mostly males affected |
| 5 | X-linked dominant inheritance | Vitamin-D-resistant rickets — affected father passes it to ALL daughters |
| 6 | Y-linkage | Only father-to-son; e.g., hairy ears trait |
| 7 | Lyonisation | One X in each female cell is inactivated — the Barr body |

**Sex determination systems across organisms**

| Organism / group | System | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Humans, most mammals | XX / XY | Y chromosome with SRY determines maleness |
| Birds, butterflies | ZZ / ZW | The FEMALE is the heterogametic sex (ZW) |
| Honeybee | Haplodiploidy | Fertilised eggs (2n) = females; unfertilised (n) = males |
| Some reptiles (turtle, crocodile) | Temperature-dependent | Incubation temperature of the egg decides sex |
| Drosophila | XX / XY | Sex is set by the RATIO of X chromosomes to autosome sets, not by the Y |

**X-linked recessive vs X-linked dominant inheritance**

| Feature | X-linked recessive | X-linked dominant |
|---|---|---|
| Who is affected more | Males far more (only one X) | Females slightly more (two chances to inherit) |
| Carrier state | Heterozygous females are silent carriers | No silent carriers — one allele is enough |
| Affected father's sons | NONE affected (Y goes to sons) | ALL daughters affected, no sons |
| Affected father's daughters | All carriers (if mother normal) | All affected |
| Transmission pattern | Mother → son; skips generations | Can be passed by either parent |
| Examples | Haemophilia A, red-green colour blindness, Duchenne MD | Vitamin-D-resistant rickets, Rett syndrome |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A colour-blind man marries a woman with normal vision whose father was colour-blind. The woman is an obligate carrier (X^C X^c). Children: 25% colour-blind sons, 25% carrier daughters, 25% normal sons, 25% normal daughters. Note the criss-cross pattern: the son's single X came from the mother, so a colour-blind son always points to a carrier (or affected) mother — never to the father.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Why is the father, not the mother, the parent who determines a child's sex? (2) Draw the Punnett square for a carrier mother × normal father for haemophilia. (3) Why can an affected father never pass an X-linked recessive trait to his sons? (4) What is a Barr body and why do normal females have one? (5) Compare the ZZ/ZW and XX/XY systems — in birds it is the female that determines sex.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Sex in humans is chromosomal (XX/XY) with SRY as the switch. Genes on the X follow sex-linked patterns: recessive ones hit males hardest and skip generations through carrier females; dominant ones show father-to-all-daughters transmission. **Self-check:** given any pedigree, can you decide recessive vs dominant and autosomal vs X-linked from who is affected and how?

mcqs.explanation: Every NEB rule has a scope (e.g. a specific range, temperature, or sign convention); stating the condition earns full marks.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Human sex determination: XX female, XY male; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides the sex — 50:50; state 'male is heterogametic'.
Trick 2: Haemophilia pedigree: affected father X^hY passes to ALL daughters (carriers) and NO sons; carrier mother × normal father → 50% sons affected — the two standard crosses.
Trick 3: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive; females need BOTH X's affected — hence males (hemizygous) suffer far more.
Trick 4: Other disorders for the list: sickle-cell anaemia (autosomal recessive, HbS), Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner (XO), Klinefelter (XXY).
